question.prompt:
How many ordered pairs \((a, b)\) of positive integers satisfy the equation

\[ \begin{aligned} a \cdot b + 63 &= 20 \cdot \operatorname{lcm}(a, b) \\ &\quad {}+ 12 \cdot \gcd(a, b), \end{aligned} \]

where \(\gcd(a, b)\) denotes the greatest common divisor of \(a\) and \(b,\) and \(\operatorname{lcm}(a, b)\) denotes their least common multiple?

solutions.title: Factor the gcd-lcm equation
solutions.explanation:
The identity \(ab=\gcd(a,b)\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)\) lets us express the equation using just the gcd and lcm. Set
\[
x=\operatorname{lcm}(a,b),\qquad y=\gcd(a,b).
\]
Then
\[
xy+63=20x+12y,
\]
and adding the constant needed to factor gives
\[
(x-12)(y-20)=240-63=177=3\cdot59.
\]

The two factors have the same sign. They cannot both be negative: positivity of \(x,y\) would give
\[
1\le12-x\le11,\qquad 1\le20-y\le19,
\]
but every positive factorization of \(177\) has a factor at least \(59\).

Thus both factors are positive. The four ordered factor pairs of \(177\) yield
\[
(x,y)\in\{(13,197),(15,79),(71,23),(189,21)\}.
\]
The gcd must divide the lcm. The first two pairs have \(x<y\), and \(23\) does not divide \(71\). Only
\[
\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)=189=3^3\cdot7,
\qquad
\gcd(a,b)=21=3\cdot7
\]
remains.

Both \(a\) and \(b\) must have exactly one factor of \(7\). Their exponents of \(3\) must have minimum \(1\) and maximum \(3\), so those exponents are \(1\) and \(3\), in either order. No other prime can occur. Therefore the only pairs are
\[
(a,b)=(21,189),\qquad(189,21).
\]
Both work, since
\[
21\cdot189+63=4032=20\cdot189+12\cdot21.
\]
There are \(\boxed{2}\) ordered pairs, choice \(\text{B}\).
